push.lead: Same swing, same 108 km/h and 15.2° launch: with no spin the ball flies 32.1 m and goes out; at 4000 rpm topspin it lands at 22.5 m, in. A topspin ball carries an extra downward force from the moment it leaves the strings, and over 70% of the deviation happens in the second half. It never suddenly drops. You only see it in the second half.

editorial.question: Why does a topspin ball seem to suddenly dive?
editorial.thesis: A spinning ball feels the Magnus force. With topspin, the bottom of the ball turns with the airflow, so the boundary layer clings longer and is flung upward; the wake tilts up and the reaction pushes the ball down. Cross & Lindsey (2014) measured 128 new balls in flight: lift coefficients of 0.1–0.3, rising with spin. By Cross's model, at 108 km/h and 3200 rpm the downward force is about 0.41 N, against a weight of about 0.56 N for a 57 g ball: gravity effectively boosted to 1.7×. The force is there from the start and the deviation accumulates: topspin is only 0.9 m lower than no spin over the first half, but 3.1 m lower at landing. So it looks sudden.
beats: Hook: a 108 km/h forehand clears the ground by 2.5 m at the net (1.6 m above the tape) yet lands 1 m inside the baseline (model estimate)
History: Newton's 1672 letter on the curving tennis ball; Magnus's 1852 paper
Mechanism 1: with topspin the top meets the air at ~148 km/h, the bottom at ~68 km/h (model estimate)
Mechanism 2: the fuzz keeps the boundary layer turbulent; the bottom side separates later, the wake tilts up, the reaction pushes down (Cross & Lindsey, 300 fps backlit filming)
Mechanism 3: C_L 0.1–0.3; about 0.41 N at 3200 rpm vs a 0.56 N weight, ~1.7× gravity
Evidence 1: same 108 km/h and 15.2°: no spin 32.1 m, 1900 rpm 26.7 m, 3200 rpm 23.9 m, 4000 rpm 22.5 m
Evidence 2: over 70% of the deviation happens late (0.9 m → 3.1 m); same landing spot needs 7.4° vs 15.2°, landing angle 15.2° → 24.1°
Evidence 3: hard-court bounce 0.8 m vs 1.5 m, vertical speed 4.6 → 6.8 m/s
Real matches: ATP top-10 forehands average 2708 rpm; Ruud 3291, Alcaraz 3316; Nadal averages 3200, peaks near 5000
Answer + ending: replay of the opening shot. It never suddenly drops. You only see it in the second half.

editorial._assumptions: Figures marked “model estimate” are computed from Cross's published model (C_D = 0.55, C_L = 0.6·S; no wind, constant spin; hard-court bounce μ = 0.73, e_x = 0.1), not measured; each is labelled in the film.
